div.head: THE FIRST ACT
div.p: Scene: A drawing-room in O’Farrell’s house in John Street. It is very prettily but not extravagantly furnished. The O’Farrells are a young married couple of modest income.

p.hi: It is between six and seven in the evening.

div.p: Peyton, a neat parlour-maid, opens the door and shows in Mr. Davenport Barlow.

Barlow is a short, self-important person of middle age. He is very bald, red in the face, and wears a small, neatly curled moustache; he is dressed in the height of fashion. His manner is fussy and pompous. He comes forward as though he expected to find some one in the room. Seeing that it is empty, he stops and looks at Peyton. He cannot make out why there is no one to receive him.
[In a tone of surprise.] Is Mrs. O’Farrell not here?
H’m.... Will you let her know I’ve come?
Mrs. O’Farrell is not at home, sir.
Mrs. O’Farrell said, would you kindly sit down and make yourself comfortable? And I was to give you the Morning Post.
[Pompously.] I can’t imagine why Mrs. O’Farrell should think I haven’t read the Morning Post at six o’clock in the evening.
[Imperturbably.] And Mrs. O’Farrell said, will you have a whisky and soda, sir?
But when is Mrs. O’Farrell coming in?
I don’t know at all, sir.
But she telegraphed to me this afternoon, asking me to come and see her at once.
Yes, sir; I took the telegram to the post office myself.
It seems very extraordinary that she should have gone out. The matter was of considerable importance.
Very well, I’ll sit down and wait. But I can’t stay long. I’m dining at ... no matter.

[Peyton goes out. Barlow goes to a looking-glass, takes a little brush out of his pocket, and brushes his moustache. Peyton comes in again with a small tray on which are a decanter, a syphon, and a glass.
Oh, thank you. Did you say you had the Morning Post?
Yes, sir. [She hands it to him.
[Peyton goes out. Barlow helps himself to a whisky and soda, turns to the fashionable intelligence in the paper, and begins to read it with a little smile of self-satisfaction.

[Half to himself.] The Duchess of St. Erth returned to Wales yesterday. The Marchioness of Mereston has arrived at 89 Grosvenor Square. The Marchioness of Serlo and Lady Eleanor King leave for Paris this morning.

[Peyton comes in, followed by Mrs. Golightly. Mrs. Golightly is an extremely stout, good-natured lady of middle age. She is very active, but short of breath. She gives one a continual impression of having just run up a steep hill. She is Davenport Barlow’s sister.
Are you here, Davenport? Where’s Penelope?
[As if it were the most extraordinary thing in the world.] She’s out!
[She turns to Peyton with a look of inquiry.
Mrs. O’Farrell said, would you kindly sit down and make yourself comfortable, ma’am? And I was to bring you the Church Times.
[Calmly.] And Mrs. O’Farrell said, will you have a strong cup of tea, ma’am?
I’m surprised that Mrs. O’Farrell should have gone out, because she expected me.
[Handing Mrs. Golightly a paper.] Yes, ma’am.
[With a look of exasperation at Barlow.] Oh, thank you.... I think I will have a cup of tea, please.
I wonder why on earth Penelope should insist on my reading the Church Times.
I’ve just had a telegram from her.
So have I, asking me to come at once. [With a ray of light.] Perhaps we shall find some explanation in the Church Times.
Nonsense. What can the Church Times have to do with the Archduchess Anastasia?
My dear Davenport, what are you talking about?

[Peyton enters to announce Professor Golightly and immediately afterwards goes out. Golightly is a tall, spare man with grey hair, well groomed and alert. He is neatly dressed, quite tidy, and might just as well be a lawyer or a doctor as a professor of mathematics. He is clean-shaven.
Hulloa, Davenport! [To his wife.] My dear, you’re the last person I expected to find here. I thought there was a meeting of the Missionary Society at the Albert Hall.
[Peyton comes in with a tray on which are tea-things, a glass of barley-water, and a copy of the “Athenæum.”
[To Golightly.] Mrs. O’Farrell said, will you have a glass of barley-water, sir?
And I was to bring you the Athenæum. We couldn’t get this week’s, sir, but this is last week’s, and Mrs. O’Farrell hopes it will do as well.
[With a faint smile.] It’s very kind of you to have taken so much trouble.
What on earth does Penelope want me to do with last week’s Athenæum and a glass of barley-water?
Well, presumably she wants you to drink the one and to read the other.
[To his wife.] My dear, I think it’s very hard that you should have brought up our only child on the idea that my favourite form of refreshment is barley-water.
It looks as if Penelope expected you, too.
I’ve just had a wire from her.
Have you? I wonder why on earth she wired to you.
It’s so extraordinary that she shouldn’t be here. It makes me feel very nervous.
Well, frankly, I couldn’t make head or tail of it, so I jumped into a motor cab and came round from the club at once.
[Peyton comes in, followed by Beadsworth. He is a middle-aged solicitor, with a benign manner.
My dear Charles, I wish you wouldn’t be slangy. It’s gone out in our set.
[Shaking hands with Mrs. Golightly.] I’ve just had a telegram from Penelope asking me to come at once. [Turning to Peyton.] Will you let Mrs. O’Farrell know I’m here?
Mrs. O’Farrell said, would you make yourself comfortable, sir, and we’ve got the Law Times if you’d like to read it, and will you have a glass of port, sir?
[Beadsworth looks round at the others in bewilderment.
By all means have a glass of port, and I’ll swop it for my barley-water.
[Handing him the paper.] Very good, sir.
What does she want me to do with the Law Times?
I asked the same question when Peyton handed me last week’s Athenæum, and Davenport, with the perspicacity that distinguishes him, answered: read it.
Can you tell me what Penelope wants? Her telegram suggested that she wished to see me not as an old friend, but in my official capacity as the family solicitor.
I haven’t an idea. I thought her telegram most mysterious.
I wish she’d come in. I’m beginning to be dreadfully uneasy.

[Rather pompously.] I think I can put your minds at rest. I am in a position to explain the whole matter to you. The telegram she sent me makes it perfectly clear. I daresay you know that the Archduchess Anastasia is a patient of Dickie’s. And a very nice patient for him to have. I’ve never met her, though I happen to know several members of her family, and she’s a very cultivated, pleasant woman. I’ve always said to Dickie that that is the sort of practice he ought to get. The middle classes do a doctor no good.
My dear Davenport, do go on with your story.

Well, it appears that the Archduchess Anastasia has signified her desire to know Penelope. Very charming and graceful action on her part, and just like her. Of course she’s extremely grateful to Dickie for all he’s done. He’s worked a miraculous cure, and I daresay she’s heard that Penelope is my niece. It’s a maxim you can always go on: royalty knows everything. And the long and the short of it is that she’s coming to lunch here. Of course Penelope knows nothing about these matters, and in a state of great excitement she’s sent for me. It’s the best thing she could do. I can tell her everything. I’ve lived in that set all my life. It’s nothing to be particularly proud about—mere accident of birth—I happen to be a gentleman. A certain family. Well, there it is, you see.
But do you mean to say that Penelope wired all that to you? It must have cost her a perfect fortune.
She put it a little more briefly, of course, but that was the gist of it.

I can’t imagine why she should send for me because a royalty is coming to luncheon with her. It was very inconvenient to get away. I had a dozen people waiting to see me, and I was obliged to slip out by the back door in order to avoid them.
But what are the exact words of the wire she sent you, Davenport?
You can see it if you like. [Taking it from his pocket and reading.] “Come at once. Archduchess Anastasia. Penelope.”
But d’you mean to say that you made up all that story out of those three words?
Penelope knew I had a certain amount of intelligence. She didn’t want to waste her money, so she just put what was essential, and left me to gather the rest.
But my telegram says nothing about the Archduchess Anastasia.
What did Penelope say to you?
[Taking out the telegram.] “Come at once! Grave scandal! Central African Mission. Penelope.”

But that’s absurd. You know how stupid the Post Office is. They must have made a mistake. I know that the Pomeranian Royal Family is very odd, but there are limits, and I can’t imagine the Archduchess Anastasia being mixed up in a scandal with a Central African missionary.
Well, my wire merely said: “Come at once; six and eightpence. Penelope.”
Six and eightpence! Why six and eightpence?
I don’t know. That is why I lost no time in coming.

[With a twinkle.] My impression is that the Archduchess Anastasia, instead of paying Dickie’s bill for miraculously curing her, has eloped with a missionary, and Penelope, by aid of the law [with a gesture towards Beadsworth], wants to recover the money.
It’s nonsense! You’re so unpractical, Charles.
[To her husband.] But you had a telegram too, dear.
[The door is softly opened and Penelope slips in; for a moment the others do not see her, and she stands smiling at them. Golightly catches sight of her. All the others turn.]
[Coming forward and kissing Mrs. Golightly.] Good evening, mamma!
Well, papa. [She puts her face up for him to kiss.]
Oh, Mr. Beadsworth, how nice of you to come. [She shakes hands with him.] Kiss me, Uncle Davenport. [She calmly puts up her face. With some irritation he kisses her.]
Thank you.... Was your whisky and soda quite right? [Looking round.] And the port? Father, you haven’t touched the barley-water. You ungrateful old thing!
[Exasperated.] My dear, for goodness’ sake explain.
Where have you been all this time?
I—I’ve been sitting in the consulting-room. [With a roguish smile.] I watched you all come in.
[Rather injured.] Peyton said you were out.
Really, Penelope, I think your behaviour is outrageous.
You see, I thought if I saw you one after the other as you came in, I should have to make four scenes instead of one. It would have been very exhausting and not nearly so effective.
Are you going to make a scene?
[With the greatest satisfaction.] I’m going to make a dreadful scene in a minute.
Now, my dear, before you go any further, for goodness’ sake tell us what you meant by your telegrams.
Well, you see, I wanted you all to come immediately, and I thought the best thing was to trail your ruling passions under your noses.
Do you understand what she means, Charles?

My dear mother, it’s the simplest thing in the world. You spend your life in converting the heathen—from a distance—and I knew if I mentioned the Central African Mission you’d fly here on the wings of the wind.
In point of fact I came in an omnibus. But do you mean to tell me that there has been no scandal in connection with the Central African Mission?
[Smiling.] I’m dreadfully sorry to disappoint you, mother.
And what in heaven’s name made you wire decimal 7035 to me?
Oh, that’s our telephone number, and I just put decimal instead of Gerrard.
I thought the figures were strangely familiar.
And there you are, you see.
[Chuckling.] I think it’s a capital idea. And she just flung the words six and eightpence at you, Beadsworth, and knew she’d fetch the lawyer.
[To Beadsworth.] You’re not cross with me, are you?
And now, my dear, that you’ve disposed of them, tell me all about the Archduchess Anastasia.
[Looking at him blankly.] The Archduchess Anastasia? But I invented her.
What d’you mean, you invented her? I know her well, I’ve known her for years. I know her whole family.
[Rather embarrassed, but trying not to laugh.] Well, you see—I wanted you to come, too. And....
I don’t understand what you mean at all, Penelope. You mention one of my most intimate friends, and then you tell me you invented her.

I’m awfully sorry. I really didn’t know there was such a person, and I thought I’d made her up out of my own head.... [With a chuckle.] I think it was rather clever of me to hit upon some one you know so well.
I don’t know why you should think the mere mention of the Archduchess’s name would make me come here.

Well, you see, I know that you go out a great deal, and you know such crowds of people. I felt quite sure that if there were an Archduchess Anastasia you’d know her, and [with a wave of the hand] well, there it is you see.
[Barlow fumes silently, but does not answer.
Now, Penelope, tell us what you really do want.
[In matter-of-fact tones.] I want to divorce Dickie.
[Ruefully.] I intended to make such a scene, and now you’ve made me blurt it all out in three words.
I’ll say it again, shall I? I want to divorce Dickie.
You don’t really mean it, do you?
[Indignantly.] Of course I mean it. I’m never going to speak to him again. That’s to say, I shall have a scene with him first. I’m quite determined to have a scene with somebody.
He’s on his way home with the usual story. [With a sudden break in her voice.] Oh, if you only knew how utterably miserable I am.
My darling, is it really serious?
[Desperately.] Oh, what can I do to make you all understand?
The best way would be to begin at the beginning, and tell us all about it coherently.
[Pompously.] My dear Charles, this is not the kind of matter in which you can be of any use. You’re a mathematician, and you’re not expected to know anything about practical affairs.
[To Penelope, to ask her to speak.] Darling?
Well, the first thing is that I simply dote upon Dickie. I’ve never loved any one else, and I never shall.
That’s a very satisfactory confession after four years of matrimony.
Five years, three months, and two days. And every day I’ve loved Dickie more.
I’ve never seen a more devoted couple.
We’ve never had a quarrel. We’ve never even been cross with one another. It’s been a honeymoon that’s never come to an end.

And now I’ve discovered that he’s been lying to me for the last month. He’s been coming home dreadfully late, and when I’ve asked him where he’s been, he’s said that he had to see a patient who was very ill—such an interesting case—and it worried him so much that he was obliged to go to his club and have a rubber to settle his nerves. And the interesting case and the rubber of bridge are Ada Fergusson.
[Pompously.] But who is Ada Fergusson? I’ve never heard of her.
Ada Fergusson’s a great friend of mine. And I hate her. I always knew she was a cat. For the last four weeks Dickie’s been spending every afternoon with her from four till seven.
[Raising his eyebrows.] But do you always ask your husband where he’s been when he comes in?
[Impatiently.] My dear papa, what has that got to do with it? We all know that you’re an old dear, and the greatest mathematician in the world, but you know nothing about life at all.
Give him a sheet of paper and a pencil, Penelope, and he’ll amuse himself by doing sums while we talk the matter out.
[Pushing writing materials over to him.] There you are, papa.
But how did you find out?
[Impatiently.] Oh, what does it matter how I found out! I’ve got all sorts of proofs.
You could knock me down with a feather.
I am not in the least surprised.

I have expected it all along. You will remember, Isabel, that I was against the marriage from the beginning. I said, one doesn’t marry a doctor. One sometimes meets them in society when they’ve had their angles rubbed off a little and perhaps have been knighted, but one never meets their wives. We suppose they do marry, but they don’t marry any one we know. I may be old-fashioned, but I stick to my opinion that there are only three possible professions for a gentleman, the law, the army, and the church.
My dear Uncle Davenport, you’re talking nonsense.
[Huffily.] You ask me for my opinion, and I give it you. I regret that you should think it nonsense.
And what are you proposing to do now?
[With great determination.] I’m never going to live with Dickie again. As soon as I’ve seen him I shall leave this house for ever.
You’re proposing to have a few words with him?
Several. I’m going to tell him that I despise him, and that I hate him; I’m going to throw my wedding ring in his face, and then I shall sweep out of the room.
Have you really made up your mind that you won’t forgive him?
Nothing would induce me ever to speak to him again if it weren’t that I want to tell him exactly what I think of him.
Besides, you’ve got your family to think of. Of course you must leave him. You see, that is what I say, you’re not safe with people of no birth. I look upon all this as a blessing in disguise.
Do you wish to bring an action for judicial separation?
My dear Mr. Beadsworth, what are you talking about! I’m going to divorce him. I’m going to make an awful scandal.
Well, I suppose we could arrange that at a pinch with the help of the newspapers. Has he ever been cruel to you?

Good heavens, no! That’s what makes me so angry. The last month he’s been more perfectly charming and delightful than ever. Oh, I wish I could do something really unpleasant to Ada Fergusson. Something with boiling oil in it.
I am shocked, frankly shocked. I would never have thought that Dickie could be so wicked.
Family life in England is going to the dogs. That is the long and short of it.
[Suddenly Penelope catches sight of what Golightly has been diligently writing. She gives the paper a startled look and then turns round.
Mother, a dreadful thing has happened. Papa has suddenly become a drivelling lunatic.
My dear, what are you saying?
He’s been adding two and two together all over that piece of paper, and he makes it five every time.
Two and two are five. Two and two are five.
Two and two are five. Two and two are five.
I knew this would happen. I’ve been expecting it for years.
Papa, you don’t really think that two and two are five?
On the contrary, I’m convinced that two and two are four.
Then why on earth have you made it five?
Do you know why you buy Pears’ soap?
I expect you’ve been working too hard, father dear. Why don’t you go and lie down for half an hour? And when Dickie comes in he’ll give you a tonic.
You buy Pears’ soap because you’re told on fifty thousand hoardings that it’s matchless for the complexion.
That’s not funny, papa, that’s silly.
You’ve only got to say a thing often enough, and all the world will believe it. And when the world believes it, it’s very hard to say if it’s true or not.
What has that got to do with two and two?
I thought if I wrote “two and two are five” often enough I might come to think it true.
But if you wrote it a million times it wouldn’t be any truer.
That is the conclusion I’m regretfully forced to.
The whole of life is merely a matter of adding two and two together and getting the right answer.

My dear Charles, if you’re going to discuss life I think there’s no need for me to stay. I’ve told you for twenty years that you’re a scholar and a recluse. I have lived in the world, and I’m a practical man. If Penelope wants to consult me, I am at her service; if not....
During the last five years I’ve seen you adding two and two together and making them about seventy-nine.
I don’t know what you’re talking about, Charles. Dickie’s behaviour is abominable, and there are no excuses for him. It’s a mere matter of common morality.
My dear, I have no objection to you talking common morality if you’ll let me talk common sense.
My dear Charles, they’re the same thing.
If you think you can make me forgive Dickie by telling me that you were a wicked old thing yourself in your youth, I may as well tell you at once that it won’t wash.
[Outraged.] What are you talking about, my dear?
Well, I’ve noticed that when a woman discovers that her husband has been unfaithful, her male relations invariably try to console her by telling her how shockingly they’ve treated their own wives.
My dear, I was going to confess nothing of the sort. I never confess.
Of course, if it were the other way about, and mamma had kicked over the traces a little....
Darling, can you see me performing an acrobatic feat of that character?
I think you’ve treated Dickie shamefully.
If your mother had behaved to me as you’ve behaved to Dickie, I should certainly have taken to drink.
But I’ve been a perfect angel. I’ve simply worshipped the ground he walked on. I’ve loved him as no man was ever loved before.

My dear, you’ve loved him morning, noon, and night. You’ve loved him when he talked, and you’ve loved him when he was silent. You’ve loved him walking, you’ve loved him eating, you’ve loved him sleeping. He’s never been able to escape from your love.
You need not have shown it.
And do you mean to say that justifies him in philandering with Ada Fergusson?
No; but strange as it may seem to you, they’re human beings. When you were a child you doted on strawberry ices.
Would you like to eat strawberry ice for breakfast, lunch, tea, and dinner every day for a month?
Good heavens! the thought fills me with horror.
Poor Dickie has lived on strawberry ice for five years. It’s been his only means of sustenance.

You’ve never let him go out without coming into the hall to put on his hat and kiss him good-bye; he’s never come into the house without you running down to help him off with his coat and kiss him welcome. When he sat down after breakfast in the morning to read his paper and smoke his pipe, I’ve seen you sit down on the arm of his chair and put your arm round his neck.
Do you think it was very awful?
[To Beadsworth.] Did Mrs. Beadsworth never sit on the arm of your chair when you were smoking your pipe?
I must confess I’m thankful my wife occupied those moments in attending to her household duties.
You are a lot of horrid old things. I ask you to come here to sympathise with me, and you’re perfectly brutal to me.
My dear Penelope, there are limits.
Well, I don’t care; I’m going to divorce him.
Let’s do another little simple addition, shall we? Perhaps two and two will make four a second time.
I don’t know that I much like being a mathematician’s daughter.
Don’t you think, instead of divorcing your husband, it would be better to win back his affection?
[Smiling.] Are you sure you wouldn’t if you could get it?
[Penelope looks at her father for a moment, then goes up to him quickly.

[With tears in her voice.] Papa, d’you think I ever could win back his love? You say I’ve lost it through my own fault. Oh, I don’t know what to do without him. I’ve been so wretched since I knew. I’ve tried to put a cheerful face on it, but if you knew what I feel in my heart.... Oh, the brutes, why didn’t they hide it from me?
My dear Penelope, I expected you to have more spirit. He’s a person of no family. I should have thought you were well rid of him.
Uncle Davenport, if you say a word against him, I will immediately have an attack of hysterics.
What you expect your father to be able to tell you I can’t imagine.
[Smiling.] Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings, Davenport....
I shouldn’t have thought one could describe you as either. But, in any case, I can stay no longer.
Oh, no, don’t go yet, Uncle Davenport.
It appears that my advice is not wanted, and I promised to look in on dear Lady Hollington before dinner.
Do telephone to her that you can’t come. You’ll find a telephone in my sitting-room.
[Shrugging his shoulders.] I’m too indulgent. People don’t rate me at my proper value.
Papa, say you’ll get Dickie back for me. I want him. I want him.
My dear, it’s very simple. It merely requires a great deal of tact, a great deal of courage, and a great deal of self-control.
A good deal. You must never let yourself out of hand; you must keep guard on your tongue and your eyes and your smiles—and your temper.
I think you said it was very simple.
Is she? That makes it more serious.
If a man falls in love with a pretty woman, he falls out of it. But if he falls in love with a plain one, he’ll be in love with her all his life.
You take a load off my mind. Ada Fergusson’s extremely attractive.
Tell me exactly what to do, and I’ll do it.

It means a good deal. When he comes in, don’t make a scene, but be charming to him. For once, don’t ask him where he’s been. When he leaves you, don’t ask him where he’s going, nor at what time he’ll be back. Don’t let him know that you have the least suspicion that anything has happened. On the contrary, take every opportunity of throwing him into Ada Fergusson’s society.
Charles, you’re asking Penelope to connive at immorality.

When every difficulty disappears, Dickie will find half the savour of the intrigue gone. Half your battle is won. Leave the rest to time and Ada Fergusson. Let Ada Fergusson sit on the arm of his chair when he wants to read his paper. Let him account to Ada Fergusson for all his movements. Under such circumstances a woman is always on tenterhooks, and consequently she’s always exacting. Whenever there’s a pause in the conversation, Ada Fergusson will say, Do you care for me as much as ever you did? That speech is the rope around love’s throat. Whenever he wants to go away, Ada Fergusson will implore him to stay five minutes longer. Those five minutes that a man stays against his will are the nails in love’s coffin. Each time he leaves her Ada Fergusson will say, At what time will you be back? That question is the earth shovelled into love’s grave.
[All this while Penelope has been staring at Golightly with astonishment.
Where did you learn all this, father?
[With a deprecating shrug.] It’s a mere matter of adding two and two together, my darling.
I had no idea that mathematics were so interesting—nor so immoral.
What do you think of it?
But if Dickie falls out of love with Ada Fergusson there’s no reason why he should fall in love again with me.
It only requires a little more tact, a little more courage, and a little more self-control.
But if I acquire so many virtues I shan’t be a woman, but a monster, and how can he love me then?
[From the window.] There’s a car stopping at the door.
Listen.... I can hear a key being turned. It must be Dickie.
What are you going to do?
My dear, I highly disapprove of your father’s idea, and I can’t imagine how it ever came into his head, but I’m bound to say I think there’s some sense in it.
[Making up her mind.] I’ll try. Remember, no one knows anything that has happened. You’ll back me up, mamma, won’t you?
You’re not going to ask me to tell a pack of lies, darling?
Only white ones, mother. If there’s a whopper to tell, I’ll tell it myself.
He’s a man of the world. He’s sure to put his foot in it.
I could not get on to her. I don’t know what’s the matter with those telephone girls. Hussies!
Uncle Davenport, I find I’ve been entirely mistaken about Dickie. He’s not to blame in any way.
Good gracious me! And Ada Fergusson?
Is, I have no doubt, no worse than anybody else.
This is a surprise. How on earth have you come to this conclusion?
By adding two and two together.
Upon my word! I must say, it annoys me that I should have been forced to break an important engagement for no reason. I should have thought....
[Interrupting.] Uncle Davenport, it’s quite bad enough that I should be done out of a scene, but if you’re going to make one it’s more than I can stand.
Well, as I can’t be of any more use to you, I think I’ll get back to the bosom of my family.
Of course, I look upon this as a professional visit.
I couldn’t dream of accepting your services for nothing. You must really let me know what I owe you.
I really don’t know what to say.
Dickie charges a guinea when he goes to see anybody.
You only mentioned six and eightpence in your telegram.
Very well, I’ll owe you that. It would really make me feel more comfortable.
You’re not going to hand it over in hard cash?
I wasn’t thinking of paying you. But I’d like to think I owed it you. You see, then, I shan’t feel under any obligation.
In that case I surrender. Good-bye.
Good-bye, Beadsworth. You must come and dine with me at the club one of these days.
Very nice fellow. Quite a gentleman. No one would think he was a solicitor. I shall ask him to dinner with one or two people who don’t matter.
There’s Dickie. D’you hear him whistling? He’s evidently in the best of spirits.

[Dickie comes in. He is a good-looking, well-dressed, professional man of five-and-thirty. He has boisterous spirits and high good humour. He is seldom put out of countenance. He has a charm of manner which explains Penelope’s infatuation.
Hulloa! I couldn’t make out what had become of you, Pen.
You generally come down to meet me when I get in.
[Penelope gives a slight start and conceals a smile.
[Gaily.] That’s no reason why you should neglect a devoted husband. [Shaking hands with Mrs. Golightly.] How is your sainted mother? Hulloa, Uncle Davenport, what price duchesses to-day?
I beg your pardon. I don’t know what you mean.
[Looking round at the decanters and glasses with which the room is scattered.] I say, you’ve been doing yourselves rather proud, haven’t you? Who’s been drinking port?

That’s how providence behaves to me. Deliberately puts temptation in my way. It’s simply poison. Gout in my family, you know. My ancestors have lived on colchicum for a hundred years. I feel a tingling in my toes at the mere sight of a bottle of port. And yet I drink it.
[He fills himself a glass and sips it with great content.
It’s a great mistake, of course, to think that gout is a mark of good family. The porter of my club is a martyr to it.
Perhaps he’s the illegitimate son of an earl. You should ask him if he has a strawberry mark on his left shoulder. What’s the matter, Pen?
I thought you seemed a bit under the weather.
I don’t know. You’re not quite up to your usual form, are you? You’ve not asked me what I’ve been doing to-day. As a rule you’re so interested in my movements.
[With a glance at her father.] I thought you’d tell me if you wanted to.
I say, I do think that’s a bit thick. I go slaving my very soul out to provide you with a motor and nice frocks and things, and you don’t take the smallest interest in what I do.
[Smiling.] Well, what have you been doing this afternoon?

[With a sigh of relief.] Oh, I’ve had the very deuce of a day. I’ve got a very interesting case on just now. Taking up a lot of my time. Of course, it worries me rather, but I suppose all these things come in the day’s march. Well, I spent the best part of an hour there.
Yes, we had a consultation, you know.
But you had a consultation yesterday.
Yesterday? Yes, she’s a fussy old thing. She’s always wanting consultations.
I don’t think it is. It looks as if she hadn’t really confidence in me.
On the other hand, you can charge double, can’t you?
Yes, of course, it has that advantage.
I’ve been hankering after an ermine stole for a long time. I shall buy it now.
[His face falling.] Oh, but I haven’t been paid yet.
They’ll be only too glad to wait. And it’s such a bargain.
[To change the conversation.] Well, after my consultation I was so fagged that I had to go into the club to have a rubber of Bridge.
By the way, what is the name of your patient?
Oh, yes, I was telling papa that you’d got a new patient who was bringing in pots of money. I couldn’t remember her name.
How d’you mean, Mrs. Macnothing? I’ve never heard of a family called Macnothing.
No, of course, her name isn’t Macnothing.
But you distinctly said it was Mrs. Macnothing.
Now, my dear Pen, did I say anything about Macnothing?
Well, what is her name then?
I’ve been telling you for the last ten minutes. Her name’s Mrs. Mack.
Why on earth didn’t you say so at once?
How did you find such a profitable patient?
Oh, it was a great piece of luck. She heard about me from that little friend of yours, Pen. What is her name?
You seem to have a very bad memory for names, Dickie. You should make a knot in your handkerchief.
It’s a friend of Pen’s. [Pretending to try and remember.] Her husband’s in the navy, stationed at Malta, isn’t he?
That’s it, of course. Mrs. Fergusson.
One of the Fergussons of Kingarth, I suppose?
I don’t know at all. Quite a nice little thing, I thought. I must confess that she didn’t interest me very much.
[Peyton comes in to announce Mrs. Fergusson. Mrs. Fergusson is a handsome, showy woman of about thirty.
[Dickie is filled with consternation. Peyton goes out. There is a very brief moment of embarrassment, but Penelope quickly recovers herself and goes up to the visitor effusively.
Is it a preposterous hour to pay a call?
Of course not. I’m always delighted to see you.
I’ve been shopping the whole afternoon, and it suddenly occurred to me that I hadn’t seen you for ages.
Do you know my sainted mother?
This is my noble father, and this is my uncle.
[He is evidently much struck by Mrs. Fergusson.
[Turning blandly to Dickie.] You haven’t forgotten me?
We haven’t met for ages, have we?
I passed you in Piccadilly the other day, and you cut me dead.
I’m so sorry, I’m so short-sighted.
Dickie, you’re not at all short-sighted. How can you tell such fibs?
[With pompous gallantry.] Dickie feels that only a physical impediment can excuse a man for not seeing a pretty woman.
Oh, how very nice of you to say that.
Not at all, not at all.
I wanted to thank you for getting Dickie such a splendid patient.
[Hastily, seeing her look of astonishment.] I’ve just been telling my wife about Mrs. Mack.
[Not in the least understanding.] Oh, yes.
It was really awfully good of you to tell her to send for me. I’ve been to see her this afternoon.
[Understanding.] Oh, yes. I like to do all I can for people. I hope you’ll find her a nice patient.
She seems to require a lot of visits.
Yes, she was only telling me the other day how much she liked Dr. O’Farrell. I’m afraid she’s very ill, poor dear.
To tell you the truth, I’m extremely worried about her.
It’s a great comfort to all her friends to know that Dr. O’Farrell is looking after her.
I’ve been wondering if she’s one of the Staffordshire Macks or one of the Somersetshire Macks.
How d’you mean you don’t know at all? She must be one or the other.
I don’t see that it matters either way.
Oh, I don’t know. Like everybody else, I suppose.
Don’t be silly, Dickie. You must know if she’s fat or thin.
[Looking at Mrs. Fergusson.] I should say fat, wouldn’t you?
[Laughing.] Yes. I wonder how she does them.
She has very pretty blue eyes, hasn’t she?
Catherine Mack? Mother, it’s your old friend Catherine Mack. What an extraordinary coincidence!
Catherine Mack. Why, of course, I remember her perfectly. Little grey corkscrew curls and very pretty blue eyes.
Wouldn’t she like mamma to go and see her?
I’m afraid she can’t see any one just yet.
You must tell her how sorry we are to hear she’s so ill.
Oh, yes, I’ll give her any message you like.
[Rather stiffly, getting up.] I think I ought to be going. Will you come, Charles?
[They talk aside as Mrs. Golightly is helped on with her cloak. Dickie is left practically alone with Mrs. Fergusson.
[In an undertone.] I say, what the dickens have you come here for now?
You didn’t tell me when I should see you to-morrow.
Good heavens, you might have rung me up on the telephone.
Oh, I never trust the telephone.
How do you mean you never trust the telephone? Are you in the habit....
I beg your pardon, I didn’t mean that.
Why on earth did you invent that cock-and-bull story about Mrs. Mack?
I didn’t. It invented itself. I was obliged to account for my movements.
D’you mean to say your wife asks you where you’ve been and where you’re going? How like a woman. [Innocently.] By the way, what are you doing this evening?
[With amusement.] Oh, Penelope and I are dining at the Carlton grill room, and going to a music hall.
[To Penelope, as he shakes hands with her.] Devilish fine woman.
[As he is following.] Are you all right?
Yes, leave it to me. I’m beginning to feel my feet.
Charming man your uncle is, Penelope. So distinguished.
You’ve made a conquest of him. He told me you were a devilish fine woman.
Not really? Men often tell me I’m a womanly woman.
I daresay it means the same thing.
But I must fly too. I really had no idea it was so late.
Oh, no! I live very quietly. There’s nothing that I enjoy more than an evening all by myself, with a book.
You used to be so fond of going out.
I know that my husband prefers me to remain at home. And when I think of him bravely serving his country in a foreign land I have no heart for gaiety.
What a charming nature you have.
[To Dickie.] My husband’s in a man-of-war. He’s stationed at Malta, you know. It’s so dreadful that my health forces me to remain in England.
I wonder if you’d do me a great kindness.
My dear, I’ll always do anything for an old friend.
The fact is, I’ve had a perfectly fiendish headache the whole afternoon.
[Triumphantly.] I knew there was something the matter with you the moment I came in.
We’ve got a couple of stalls for a music hall to-night. It would be awfully kind of you if you’d go with Dickie instead of me.
[A look of intelligence passes between Dickie and Mrs. Fergusson.
Dickie hates going out alone, and I simply can’t stir. You can have a jolly little dinner together at a restaurant, and you can go on afterwards.
Are you really sure you can’t go, Pen?
It’s absolutely out of the question.
Don’t you think Dr. O’Farrell ought to stay and look after you?
Oh, no! It’ll do him good to go out. He’s been working so dreadfully hard. This afternoon he had a consultation that lasted nearly an hour.
[To Dickie.] Would you like me to come with you?
I should love it, if it wouldn’t bore you.
Thanks so much. But it’s getting very late. I think you ought to start at once.
You’re sure you don’t mind my leaving you, Penelope?
Well, just wait a moment, and I’ll make you up a dose of something.
[Hastily.] Oh, no, I promise you I’m much better without medicine.
Nonsense. Of course I must give you something.
That’s the advantage of having a doctor in the family.
I do envy you, having your husband always at hand. When I think of mine bravely serving his country—and you know, every doctor I go to tells me it would be most dangerous for me to join him.
[Dickie comes in with a little medicine glass, filled with a milky fluid.
Oh, no, Dickie, I’d much rather not.
Don’t be silly, darling. This’ll pull you together like anything.
I’m sure she ought to lie down.
No, I think I’d rather stand up if you don’t mind.
How extraordinarily unreasonable you are! Now lie down on this sofa.
Of course, if I absolutely must.
We must make you comfortable before we go.
Let’s put all the cushions behind her. Is that nice?
I’m sure she ought to have something over her feet.
Let’s put this rug over her feet. There. Now take this medicine.... There....
Oh, no, Dickie. I’ll take it after you’ve gone. I really will. I promise you I’ll take it.
Why on earth can’t you take it now?
Well, I hate making faces before you.
But I’ve often seen you make faces.
Yes, at you. That’s quite a different thing.
Now, take it like a good girl.
[With great determination.] I’m not going to stir from this room till you’ve taken it.
[Resigned.] Give it me. Hold my nose, Dickie.
[She swallows it and makes a face.
Oh, I wish I’d never married you, Dickie.
It’ll make you feel like one o’clock.
I don’t want to feel like one o’clock.
Good-bye. So sorry you’re feeling seedy.
I hope you’ll have an awfully good time.
[Dickie and Mrs. Fergusson go out. Penelope springs up, throws the cushions angrily aside, makes one or two quick steps towards the door as though to call them back, then stops.
[She comes slowly back, then sinks down and bursts into tears.

div.head: THE SECOND ACT
div.p: Scene: Dr. O’Farrell’s consulting-room. It is a comfortably furnished room, with engravings on the walls, photographs in silver frames, and flowers on the chimney-piece. There is a large desk on one side, with papers on it, books, and a reading-lamp. There is a revolving-chair for Dickie to sit in, and a chair on the other side of the desk for the patient. On a side table are a microscope, a stand for test tubes, one or two medicine bottles, a row of large bottles containing chemicals, and an electric lamp. There is a sofa without arms for patients to lie upon, and there are two or three chairs besides. On the shelves are medical books. On a little table is a pile of “Lancets.”

Dickie is sitting at his desk, with his stethoscope still in his ears. A patient is standing up, buttoning up his braces. He puts on his waistcoat and coat as the conversation proceeds. He is a very timid little man, with a bald head and gold spectacles. He has an intensely nervous, apologetic manner.
I’ll just write you out a prescription, shall I?
Oh, it’s too good of you. I’m afraid I’m giving you so much trouble.
Not at all. Now what would you like me to give you?
[Dreadfully embarrassed.] Oh, whatever you like, please. It’s too good of you.
You know, there’s not much the matter with you.
Oh, I’m so sorry. I really, really....
I should have thought you’d be rather pleased.
[Apologetically.] Yes, of course, I’m very much pleased. I didn’t mean that. I’ve taken up so much of your time.
It’s only out of the people who’ve got nothing the matter with them that I make a living. The people who are ill either get well or die, and that’s the end of them.
Yes, I see. I never thought of that. Beautiful day it is, isn’t it?
Oh, it’s too good of you. Thank you, thank you. I’m afraid I’m taking up so much of your time.

I always make my patients sit on the other side of my desk since one of them suddenly saw a snake on me, and flung himself at my throat in order to save me from being bitten. He nearly throttled me in the process, and when I knelt on his chest, he said I was an ungrateful devil, and he wouldn’t interfere with the snakes next time they went for me.
[Extremely agitated.] Oh, but you don’t think there’s any danger of my flying at your throat, do you?
[With a laugh.] No, of course not.
I drink nothing for my luncheon, and only claret and water for my dinner.
I suppose you wouldn’t think you’d had your money’s worth if I gave you no medicine?
Oh, it’s too good of you, but I think, for my wife’s sake, I’d like to take something.
Well, look here, I’ve given you some strychnine to buck you up, and some bismuth to quiet you down. Take it three times a day after meals.
Oh, thank you so much. I’m sure it’s just what I want. And now—er. And now—er....
I think there’s nothing more I can do for you.
No, er—thank you very much. I—er—it’s so good of you to have taken so much trouble. Yes, er....
[Understanding.] Oh.... My fee is two guineas.
[Infinitely relieved.] Oh, thank you so much. That’s just what I wanted to ask you. Shall I write you a cheque?
We always prefer to have it in hard cash, you know, in case it’s a bogus cheque.
Oh, certainly. It’s too good of you. I thought you mightn’t like it.
It’s extraordinary how nervous people are about giving a doctor money. If you only knew how jolly glad he is to get it.
[The patient takes two guineas out of his pocket and puts them nervously on the chimney-piece.
Hang it all, man, not on the mantelpiece. There are limits.
Oh, I beg your pardon. I’m so sorry.
We always like it put on the desk.
I don’t often come and consult doctors.
I can see that. If you did you’d probably give me two pounds and say you hadn’t got two shillings on you, especially if you were a woman.
You don’t say so. Really it never occurred to me.
Good-bye, and thank you so much. Beautiful day, isn’t it? Good-bye.
[Dickie leads him to the door and shows him out. At the door he sees Golightly.
Hulloa! Come in, won’t you? [Calling upstairs.] Pen, here’s your noble parent.
I was just going up to see Pen.
Come and sit down here, and we’ll have a smoke.
Oh, it’s just on five o’clock. I don’t suppose any one else will come. We might have tea down here.
Rotten. Look here, a wretched two guineas. That’s all I’ve made this afternoon.
Kiss your noble parent, my child. You’ve got a new dress on.
I rather like it, don’t you?
Is that another new frock, Pen?
The wife of a fashionable physician has to spend a lot of money on her clothes.
Dickie was lamenting that times were very bad.

What can you expect with this beastly weather! Fine, dry, cold day after day. We haven’t had a fog this autumn. It doesn’t give one a chance. Of course everybody keeps well. Times are getting worse and worse. Everybody has decent drains now. An officious Government gives people pure water. If it weren’t for patent medicines and the malade imaginaire half the doctors in London would starve.
Never mind, Dickie. There may be a motor accident just outside our front door one of these days.
It would be just like my luck if they were all killed outright. No, what I want is a really good epidemic, a very complicated form of influenza that’d keep people on their backs for about a month.
Well, if you got it that bounder on the other side of the street would have to treat you. And he couldn’t charge you as you’re my wife, and he’d simply grind his teeth at having to waste his time.
The bounder on the other side of the street is Dr. Rogers. I like him much better than Dickie.
He’s got such a pleasant bedside manner.
You’ve never seen my bedside manner. [Looking at his hands.] I say, I must just go and wash my hands, they’re covered with Picric Acid.
From the safe distance of the Albert Hall.
[With a change of manner.] I’m glad you came alone.
[Breaking out.] I can’t go on with it any longer. I’ve come to the end of my strength.
Yes. I can’t imagine what he sees in her. I sit and watch her sometimes and wonder what she has that I haven’t got. You don’t think I’m plain, do you?
Certainly not. If you had been I should have exposed you at your birth, like the ancient Spartans.
There are lots of men who are willing to tell me that I’m extremely attractive.
My dear father, you’re the most immoral parent I’ve ever come across.
[With a little deprecatory shrug.] It might be politic.

[Shaking her head.] No, I don’t know whether I shall ever get Dickie back again, but I don’t want to get him back by exciting his jealousy. I don’t want his love if I can only have it by making him think other men are in love with me.
Remember that two and two never make five.
[Impatiently.] It’s easy enough to give advice. You’ve only got to sit still and watch. I’ve got to do things. And the worst of it is that doing things means doing nothing.

Now, father, don’t look as if you didn’t understand or I shall throw something at your head. It wouldn’t be so bad if I could be up and doing, but I just have to sit still and keep my temper. You don’t know what I’ve suffered this month with a smiling face. I’ve laughed while my heart ached. I’ve chaffed Dickie when I’ve known he was just going to meet Ada Fergusson. I’ve arranged little parties so that they might be together. I haven’t even dared to cry by myself in case Ada Fergusson should see that my eyes were red and tell Dickie. He’s seen her every day, every single day for the last month, and all the time I’ve been cheerful and pleasant and amusing.
But how does he manage to get the time?
Of course he’s been neglecting his practice. He’s sent his assistant to people he ought to have seen himself. You remember Mrs. Mack, don’t you?
If you knew how I hated Mrs. Mack! She’s been having operations. She has an operation about once a week, and Dickie goes off for the whole day in his car.
She must have the constitution of a boa-constrictor.

And the curious thing is that she always has an operation when there’s a race meeting. She had an operation for the Duke of York’s Stakes at Kempton; and she had another operation for the Cesarewitch, and a third for Sandown.

It is till you know that Ada Fergusson adores racing. And the thing that makes me so furious is that I’m quite certain Dickie puts on her money for her; and when her horse wins she pockets the profits, and when it loses she doesn’t pay her stake.
That sounds very nasty of her. What makes you think it?
I do it myself.... Poor Dickie, it’s going to cost him a lot of money this month.
Because whenever he goes out for the day I have to console myself by buying something. I generally choose something rather dear.
I don’t remember that I advised that in the treatment of a volatile husband.
No, I added it of my own accord.
But why did you send for me to-day?

Because the end has come. And I can’t stand it any longer. This morning Dickie said that Mrs. Mack was well enough to be moved, and he was going to take her over to Paris to put her in the Riviera train.
Do you mean to say that....
[With an angry shrug of the shoulders.] Ada Fergusson wants a little jaunt in Paris.
What are you going to do?
I’m going to tell him he must choose between us. I’m going to do everything I can to prevent him from going. And I mean to let him know that if he goes it’s the end.
Don’t say oh! Say I’m quite right. Say it’s the only thing to do.
But I think you’re quite wrong.
You don’t suppose he wants to go to Paris. No man in his senses would take the risk.
Because she’s making him. And once a woman in these circumstances makes a man do what he doesn’t want to, it’s the beginning of the end.
I don’t know. I guess it.
It seems to me that a lifetime spent in the study of mathematics has resulted in some very various knowledge.
Be a good girl, Pen, and let them go.
[There is a pause while Penelope, resting her face on her hands, looks straight at her father. She thinks the matter out.
You were right when you said I should want a great deal of tact, and a great deal of patience, and a great deal of self-control. My word!
I’ll do nothing. I’ll hold my tongue, I’ll smile, I’ll make jokes, but....
I want some hats badly. I’ll just go and ring up Françoise and tell her to send me all she’s got in the shop.
I promised to fetch my wife.
You must come back. This is the first time I’ve been separated from Dickie since our marriage, and I shall want to hide my head in the maternal bosom while my noble father pats my hand.
I wish you wouldn’t take it so calmly, Pen. You might be a bit cut up.
But, darling, I’m making every preparation to have fit after fit of violent hysterics. I can’t do more.
[With meaning.] After all, Dickie, I know you wouldn’t go if you could help it. It’s only because you feel it’s your duty, isn’t it?
[Dickie is rather uncomfortable, but says nothing. Golightly breaks the momentary silence.
Why are you going by night?
[Relieved.] Oh, you see, there’s so much less of a crowd. It’s more convenient when you’re carting an invalid about.

[Gaily.] It’ll be great fun, because you’ll see all the gay young men who are making a little excursion to Paris with the object of their affections. I’m told they always go by night so that no one should see them on the journey.
Well, I must be getting on or I shall be late. Au revoir.
Don’t be too long, father, in case my emotions get the better of me before you come back.
[Nodding.] I may see you later, Dickie.
[He goes out. Penelope makes as if to follow him.
I’m going upstairs to have tea.
[Rather stiffly.] I’d like to have a little talk with you, Pen.
Then come up into the drawing-room.
I’d rather talk to you down here.
You can send for the tea if you like.
No; I’ll let it stand and ruin my digestion.
[Taking papers out of his pocket and giving them to Penelope.] D’you know what these are?
I can see they’re bills, thank you!
[Flourishing one of them.] This is for the frock I’ve got on. You wouldn’t think it cost so much, would you? [Looking down at it.] You see, you have to pay for the cut.
[Trying to keep his temper.] And what do you expect me to do with them?
[Indifferently.] You can put them in the waste-paper basket if you like, but it would be shorter to pay them.
[Flying into a passion.] Now, look here, Pen. It’s perfectly preposterous. You know I’m not going to stand this sort of thing.

[Apparently much astonished, quite good-humouredly.] Darling, you’re not going to make a scene for a few little things I’ve bought myself. I was positively in rags, and I thought you liked me to dress neatly.
Hang it all, I’m a poor man, and you’ve spent more than a hundred and fifty pounds in this one month.
[Calmly.] Does it come to as much as that? It’s lucky you’ve got such a good patient in Mrs. Mack, isn’t it?
[He gives her a suspicious look, but to get away from Mrs. Mack breaks out angrily.
Senseless extravagance I call it. Now look here, here’s thirty-five pounds for a dress in blue cloth—absurd price to pay—on 9th of October.
Duke of York’s Stakes at Kempton.
How d’you mean, Duke of York’s Stakes at Kempton?
I just happen to remember they were on that day because Madame Claude was so surprised to see me. It was only by the merest chance that she hadn’t gone to the races herself.
But what on earth put it into your head to go and buy a blue cloth dress?

[Sweetly.] Well, you see, darling, it was the day of the first operation that was performed on Mrs. Mack. And you were away all day, and I felt awfully depressed and lonely. And I knew how anxious you were, and it made me anxious, so I just went and ordered a blue cloth to cheer myself up a bit.
[Dickie looks at her for a moment, then looks down at the bill, is about to speak, but says nothing. Penelope watches him.
[Suddenly.] And look here, on the 13th of October there’s an ermine stole and a muff.
Yes, that was the second operation on poor Mrs. Mack.
I say, I think it’s a bit thick.
Well, I had to do something while you were away. And it made me feel so miserable to see everybody driving off with race glasses to Liverpool Street.
You see, the 13th of October was the Cesarewitch.
And I suppose all the others are to be explained in the same way. [Looking at a bill.] October 22.
[Dickie looks through the bill crossly, but does not speak.
[Innocently.] I wonder why you always had your operations on the same day as an important race meeting.
I suppose you think it odd?

Well, it isn’t odd at all. It’s one of old Peter Marsden’s cranky ways. I told you it was Peter Marsden who did the operations, didn’t I? [Penelope nods.] The fact is, he’s simply mad on racing. And he’s lost such a pot of money that he always fixes an important operation for the same day as a race meeting so that he absolutely won’t be able to go to it.
[With a laugh.] Peter Marsden, not you, darling.
Now look here, Pen, we’ll say no more about these bills. I’ll pay them this time....
But there must be no more of them.
I really don’t know why you should make such a fuss. After all, you’ve been earning simply heaps and heaps of money with Mrs. Mack.
We mustn’t count our chickens before they’re hatched. I haven’t had a penny out of her yet.
But now that she’s going away you can send in your bill.
Oh, I couldn’t possibly. It would kill her.
Don’t you think you might risk it?
I think you’re awfully heartless, Pen. You forget that I’m very much attached to the old lady. I look upon her as a friend as well as a patient.
Perhaps she’ll leave you something in her will. We want a new electric brougham, don’t we?
Oh, I shouldn’t accept it. I have the strongest feeling against doctors getting legacies from their patients.
Well, you’ll be able to charge at least a hundred and fifty pounds for taking her to Paris.
You’re not proposing to buy anything more?
Well, darling, I know that when I get up to-morrow morning and you’re not here, I shall feel dreadfully lonely and depressed.
[Interrupting.] Have your sainted mother to stay with you.
And it’s struck me that I simply haven’t got a hat I can wear.
[Persuasively.] It’ll make my frocks last so much longer if I have some nice hats. You see, you ring the changes, and people think you have a new gown on.
And may I venture to inquire how many hats you’ll want to overcome your depression?
I never heard anything so preposterous.
Now look here, Dickie, I’m willing to meet you half way; I promise you they shan’t cost more than five pounds each. You can afford that out of the hundred and fifty.
The fact is, Pen, that Mrs. Mack is more a friend than a patient, and she’s not so well to do as I thought. I’m proposing to make no charge for accompanying her to Paris.
[Quite firmly.] Oh, no, Dickie, I won’t hear of it. You’ve got a wife to think of—if you died to-morrow I should be totally unprovided for. You have no right to be quixotic. It’s not fair to me.
[Dickie is just going to answer when Peyton comes in.
A lady wishes to see you, sir.
Oh, yes, I know. Show her in.
Thank heaven, there’s somebody. I’ll get a few guineas out of her at all events. [Looking at his case book.] Four visits. That’ll be five guineas. By Jove, I want them.
I don’t know, but I’m pretending I do. And she probably won’t find out.
I’ll leave you. I must just telephone to some one.
[She goes out. Dickie walks up and down irritably. When Mrs. Watson appears he at once puts on his professional manner, and is very bland and affable. Mrs. Watson is a little, old lady in black.
You mustn’t mind my coming so late. I know you don’t see any one after five, but I’m going away.
I’m delighted to see you. I promise you that.
I’m starting for the Riviera with my daughter to-morrow, and I thought I’d like to see you again before I went.
Of course. And how have you been getting on?
[With the keenest satisfaction.] Oh! I don’t get on. I never get better.
Have you been taking your medicine regularly?
[Cheerfully.] Yes; but it doesn’t do me any good.
Let’s try your knee jerks, shall we?
[Mrs. Watson crosses one leg over the other, and Dickie taps below the knee; the leg is slightly jerked up.

Sir Benjamin Broadstairs tried everything, and he couldn’t cure me; and then I went to Sir William Wilson, and he told me not to do any of the things that Sir Benjamin Broadstairs told me to do, and I got worse and worse!
You seem uncommonly cheerful about it.

I’ve been to every doctor in London, and they all say I’m a wonderful case. I like being examined by doctors, and they take such an interest in me. The hours and hours they’ve spent over me. I can never be grateful enough for all the kindness I’ve had from them.
It’s very nice of you to say so. I think I’ll try you on something else to-day.
Oh! make it nice and strong; won’t you, doctor?
You seem to like your medicine with some body in it.

Well, I like taking medicines. It’s something to do; and now my daughter’s married I’m very much alone. I think I’ve taken every medicine in the Pharmacopœia, and they’ve none of them done me any good.
[Handing her a prescription.] Well, perhaps this will. You must take it three times a day before meals.
[Looking at it.] Oh! but I’ve had this before, Dr. O’Farrell. Sir Arthur Thomas gave me this only a few months ago.
Well, try it again. Perhaps you didn’t give it a fair chance.
I was reading in the Lancet the other day that a German doctor had discovered a new medicine which does nerve cases such a lot of good. I’m sure it’s the very thing for me.
What on earth were you reading the Lancet for?
Oh, I always read the Lancet and the British Medical Journal. You see, my poor husband had to take them in for his practice.
[With a gasp.] You don’t mean to say your husband was a doctor?
Oh, I thought I told you that I was a doctor’s widow.
[Dickie tries to master his agitation while Mrs. Watson prattles on.

I can never bear to hear doctors spoken badly of. They never do me any good, but they’ve been kindness itself. I’ve only once been rudely treated, and that—if you’ll believe it—was by a mere nobody. I told him all my symptoms, and he said to me, Madam, can you eat? Yes, I said. I have breakfast in the morning and a little soup at eleven o’clock; and then I have lunch, and I always make a good tea, and I eat a little dinner at half-past seven, and before I go to bed I have some bread and milk. Then he said, Madam, can you sleep? Yes, I said, for an old woman I sleep very well; I sleep eight or nine hours regularly. Then he said, Madam, can you walk? Oh! yes, I said, I always make a point of walking four miles a day. Then he said, My opinion is that you’ve got nothing the matter with you at all. Good afternoon.

Well, I just looked him up and down, and I said to him, Sir, your opinion is not shared by Sir Benjamin Broadstairs, or Sir William Wilson, or Sir Arthur Thomas. And I didn’t even offer him a fee, but I just swept out of the room. [Archly.] You won’t give me that new medicine?
Honestly, I don’t think it’s quite what you want.
Very well. I expect you know best. And now I mustn’t take up any more of your time.
[Sarcastically.] Oh, it’s of no value, thank you.
[Persuasively.] Will you tell me what I owe you?
Oh, as a doctor’s widow, of course, I couldn’t dream of accepting a fee.
That is kind of you. But you must allow me to give you a little present.
[Rather feebly, but brightening up a little.] Oh, really, you know....

I’ve seen every doctor in London of any importance, and they’ve none of them charged me a penny, but I always make them a little present. I know that you doctors have to go out in all weathers, and you never wrap yourselves up. So I give them a woollen comforter.
[She takes out of her bag a large red woollen comforter.
And Sir Benjamin promised to wear his every winter. You’ll find it so warm.
And now, good-bye, and thank you so much.
When you come back from the Riviera, you might do worse than consult Dr. Rogers. He lives just at the other end of the street, you know. He’s very good in cases like yours.
[She goes out, and he shuts the door. He runs to the other and calls out.
[There is a knock at the door.

I knew there was something I wanted to ask you particularly, and I nearly forgot it. Sir Benjamin Broadstairs said I ought never to eat anything but toast, and Sir William Wilson said he didn’t think toast was at all good for me, and I only ought to eat bread. Now, I wonder what I had better do?
[Seriously, as if he were deliberating.] Well, if I were you, I’d eat bread toasted only on one side.
Thank you so much. Good-bye. I hope you’ll like the comforter.
[She goes out again, and Dickie shuts the door.
[Penelope comes in by the other door.
[Dickie goes up to her furiously with the comforter in his hands.
Don’t be idiotic, Penelope. I can see it’s a woollen comforter.
But what’s the meaning of it?
She’s a doctor’s widow. Of course I couldn’t charge her anything. She kept it dark till to-day. I’ll tell you what, doctors’ widows oughtn’t to be allowed to survive their husbands.
When you’re my widow, Pen, you go right up one side of Harley Street and then right down the other and see them all.
Hang it all, when you’ve lost me the least you can do is to enjoy indifferent health.
If you please, sir, Mrs. Watson says, may she just see you for one minute.
What the dickens does she want now?
You’ll think you’ve never seen the last of me.
[Blandly.] Not at all. Not at all.
I’ve been thinking about what you said about toasting my bread on one side.... On which side shall I put the butter?
[With his chin in his hand.] H’m. H’m. You must put the butter on the toasted side.
Oh, thank you. Now just one more question, do you think a little jam would hurt me?
No, I don’t think a little jam would hurt you, but you mustn’t put it on the same side as you put the butter.
Oh, thank you. Good afternoon. I’m so much obliged.
Not at all. Not at all.
[Shaking his fist at the door.] Suttee.... That’s the word. Suttee.
Dickie, what are you talking about?
I’ve been trying to think of it for ten minutes. That’s what doctors’ widows ought to do—Suttee. Like the Hindoos.
Burn themselves alive at their husbands’ death?
You’ve hit it. Suttee. That’s the word.
But, darling, I should hate to grace your funeral by making a bonfire of myself.
Oh, you have no affection for me.
Lots, but that’s asking a great deal, isn’t it?
No, you don’t care for me as much as you used to. You’re quite different. I’ve noticed lots of things.
[With a rapid glance at him, but keeping her chaffing manner.] Oh, nonsense.

You’ve changed lately. You never come down to see me off in the morning, and you don’t ask me at what time I’m coming back. You always used to sit on the arm of my chair after breakfast when I was smoking my pipe and reading the paper.
You must have hated it, didn’t you?
Of course I hated it, but it showed you were fond of me, and now that you don’t do it any more I miss it.
[Peyton comes in, followed by Mrs. Fergusson, and withdraws.
[Dickie gives a slight start, and shows faint signs of annoyance. He cannot make out what Mrs. Fergusson has come for.
The maid told me you were here, so I asked her to show me straight in. I hope you don’t mind.
Of course not. We’re delighted to see you anywhere. Won’t you have some tea?
No, thank you. The fact is, I’ve come to see Dr. O’Farrell professionally.
I’ve not been very well lately, and I thought I’d like to see a doctor. [To Dickie.] Will you treat me?
I’ll do anything I can for you.
But it must be really a professional visit. You know, I want to pay.
Oh, nonsense, Dickie couldn’t dream of accepting money from one of my friends.
No, I’ve got the strictest principles on that point. I think it’s too bad of people to want a doctor to treat them for nothing. I really insist on paying the usual fee.
Oh, well, we’ll discuss that later.
I’ll leave you alone, shall I?
Do you mind, dear? It makes me a little uncomfortable to discuss my symptoms before a third party.
We shall only be five minutes.
I warn you that Dickie’s medicines are perfectly beastly.
I’m sorry you’re seedy. You were all right yesterday.
[Laughing.] I’ve never been better in my life, thank you.
That’s the advantage of you being a doctor. When I want to see you alone I can do it under your wife’s very nose. Don’t you think it was rather ingenious?
[She gives a little laugh. She gets up and steps cautiously to the door, and suddenly flings it open.
What on earth are you doing?
I wanted to see if Penelope was listening.
[Rather sharply.] Of course she wasn’t listening. That’s about the last thing she’d do.
Oh, my dear, don’t get in a temper about it. Lots of women do listen, you know.
Do they? I haven’t had the pleasure of meeting them.
Then will you tell me in what way I can be of use to you?
[Good-humouredly.] Certainly not, if you ask me as crossly as that. You may kiss my hand. [He does so.] That’s right. Still cross?
Do you love me as much as ever?
You wouldn’t say no if you didn’t, would you?
[Rather impatiently.] I say, what on earth have you come for?
You are nice to me to-day.
Well, when I left you yesterday we fixed up everything. I gave you your ticket, and I wrote down the time the train started.
Well, for one thing I wanted to see Penelope.

It amuses me to see her simplicity. I get a lot of pleasure in looking at her and thinking how little she suspects what is going on under her very nose. She’s the most trusting person I ever met in my life.
If you want to know anything, it makes me feel devilish uncomfortable.
My poor, dear boy, what are you talking about?

It wouldn’t be so bad if we had to take any precautions. But she trusts us absolutely. Why, she’s always throwing us together. It never enters her head that there can be the least reason for suspicion. It’s like knocking a man down who can’t defend himself.
I suppose that means that you no longer love me?
Of course I love you. Good heavens, I’ve told you so till I’m blue in the face.
Oh, no, you no longer love me. Men only begin to have scruples when they stop caring for you.
[Dickie gives a sigh of resignation. This is not the first scene he has had to put up with.
I’ve sacrificed everything for your sake. And now you insult me. And when I think of my poor husband bravely serving his country in a foreign land! Oh, it’s cruel, cruel!
But I’ve only said it made me feel low down to treat Penelope badly.
You don’t think of my feelings. You don’t think how I feel. What about my husband?
Well, you see I don’t happen to know your husband, and I do know my wife.
Don’t be so stupid. Of course you know your wife.
That’s why I don’t like behaving like an utter cad.
If you really loved me you would think of nothing but me, nothing, nothing, nothing.
[She puts her handkerchief to her eyes.
I shall cry. I’ve never been treated like this before. If you don’t love me any more, why don’t you say so?
Yes, I do love you. But....
[Nervously.] Well—er—I think it would be much better if we—put the trip to Paris off for a bit.
I’ll never speak to you again. I wish I had never met you. Oh, how can you insult me like this!
Oh, Lord! Oh, Lord! I say, don’t cry. I didn’t mean to be horrid. I’m awfully sorry.
[He tries to take away her hands from her face.
Don’t touch me. Don’t come near me.
I’ll do anything you like if you won’t cry. I say, just think if Penelope came in—I was only thinking of the risk to you. Of course, there’s nothing I’d like so much as a jaunt over the Channel.
Do you really want me to come?
Of course I do, if you don’t mind the risk.
[With a smile.] Oh, I’ll make that all right.
Why, what are you going to do?
Wait a minute or two and you’ll see.
[She is perfectly composed again, and in high good-humour.
We might tell Penelope that we’re ready.
Very well. [As Dickie goes to the door.] Oh, I quite forgot. I’ve simply got a head like a sieve.
Well, I almost forgot the very thing I came to see you about. And all through you making a scene.
Did I make a scene? I wasn’t aware of it.
I want to ask you something. You won’t be angry, will you?
Of course it’s nothing very important really, but it’s just a little awkward to ask.
Oh, nonsense. Of course I’ll do anything I can.
Well, a friend of mine on the Stock Exchange gave me a splendid tip, and....
It hasn’t come off. I know those splendid tips.
Oh, but it’s bound to be all right, only there are some differences to pay. I don’t quite understand what it all means, but Solly Abrahams....
[Interrupting.] Is that your friend on the Stock Exchange?
Oh, nothing. Good old Scotch name, that’s all.
Solly says I must send him a cheque for a hundred and eighty pounds.
[Dickie gives a slight start, and his face falls.

And it’s just a little awkward for me to pay that just now. You see my income is always paid me half-yearly, and I really haven’t got a hundred and eighty pounds in the bank. I never borrow—it’s a thing I can’t bear—and I felt the only person I could come to now was you.
I’m sure that’s awfully nice of you, not to say flattering.
I knew you’d give it me at once, and, of course, I’ll pay you back out of my profits.
Oh, that’s very good of you. I’ll see what I can do.
Would it be too much trouble if I asked you to write out a cheque now? It’ll be such a weight off my mind.
Of course. I’ll be only too glad. By the way, what are the shares called?
[He sits down at his desk and writes a cheque.
Oh, it’s a gold mine. It’s called the Johannesburg and New Jerusalem.
Thanks, so much. It’s awfully good of you. Now just write out a little prescription so as to have something to show Penelope.
And I must give you a fee.
Oh, I wouldn’t bother about that.
Oh yes, I insist. Besides, it makes it look so much more probable.
Oh, how stupid of me! I’ve only got a two-shilling bit in my purse. You don’t happen to have a couple of sovereigns on you.
Oh, yes, I think I have. The only money I’ve earned to-day.
[He takes them out of his pocket and gives them to Mrs. Fergusson. She puts them on the desk with a two-shilling piece.
Thank you.... There. That looks a most imposing fee. You must leave it on there for Penelope to see.
I will. [She goes to the door and calls.] Penelope, we’ve quite done.
[Hearing voices upstairs.] Hulloa, there’s our Uncle Davenport.
Oh, I met him in the park the other day. He made himself so pleasant. He asked me if I was a Fergusson of Glengary. I didn’t know what he meant, but I said I was, and he seemed so pleased.
You’d better not let him know you were a Miss Jones or he’ll have a fit.
Oh, I shall tell him I’m a Jones of Llandudno. I think that sounds rather smart.
You have what one might politely describe as a remarkable power of invention.
I don’t know about that, but I am a womanly woman, and that’s why men like me.
Ah, Mrs. Fergusson, this is a delightful surprise.
You wicked, wicked man, I am told you’re such a rake.
[Delighted.] Ah, ah. Tales out of school, Mrs. Fergusson.
If I’d known what a reputation you had I wouldn’t have let you talk to me for half an hour in the park.
[Bubbling over with delight.] Oh, you mustn’t listen to all you hear. A man who goes out as much as I do is sure to get talked about. Our world is so small and so censorious.
Dr. O’Farrell has been writing a prescription for me. I haven’t been very well lately.
Oh, I’m very sorry to hear that. You look the picture of health and extremely handsome.
Oh, you horrid cruel thing! I wanted you to sympathise with me and tell me how ill I looked.
If you will allow me to call on you I can promise to sympathise with you, but I’m afraid I shall never be able to tell you that you look anything but charming.
That’s too nice of you. You must come and see me the moment I get back from Paris.

I came on purpose to tell you. Really, I’ve got a head like a sieve. Poor Mrs. Mack has asked me if I would go as far as Paris with her. A most unfortunate thing has happened. Her maid’s mother has suddenly died, and the poor thing naturally wants to go to the funeral. And so....
Mrs. Mack has asked you to go in her maid’s place?
Only for two days, of course. Now, I want to know, dear, tell me honestly, do you mind?
Some women are so funny. I thought you mightn’t like the idea of my going with Dr. O’Farrell as far as Paris, and, of course, we shall be travelling back together.
What nonsense! Of course, I’m only too glad. It’ll be so nice for Dickie to have some one to travel with.
Then that settles it. I like to do everything above board, you know.
[Seeing the guineas on the desk.] I see you’ve been raking in the shekels, Dickie.
Oh, that’s my fee. I insisted on paying a fee—I particularly want you to know that, Penelope—I’m so scrupulous about that sort of thing.
Oh, but Dickie can’t accept it. [To Dickie.] You are a grasping old thing!
I’m sure I didn’t want the money.
You really must take it back, Ada.
[Putting up a defensive hand.] No, I couldn’t really. It’s one of my principles.
I know your principles are excellent, but I really shouldn’t like Dickie to accept a fee for seeing my greatest friend.
[Penelope takes up the money and gives it to Mrs. Fergusson.
Oh, well, of course, if you take it like that, I don’t know what to do.
Put it in your purse and say no more about it.
Oh, it’s too good of you.
[She puts it in her purse. Dickie’s face falls as he sees his own money disappearing.
And now I must really fly. [Holding out her hand to Barlow.] Good-bye. Don’t forget to come and see me, but, remember, I shall expect to hear all about that little ballet-girl.
[Delighted to be thought so gay.] You mustn’t ask me to be indiscreet.
I’ll come to the door with you.
[Going to the telephone.] I don’t believe you’ve ever known a ballet-girl in your life.
No, but it pleases women of our class to think one is hand and glove with persons of that profession.

Central 1234. If they only knew that nine ballet-girls out of ten go home every night to their children and a husband in the suburbs! I just want to ring up my broker. Is that you, Robertson? I say, d’you know anything about a mine called the Johannesburg and New Jerusalem? Rotten? I thought as much. That’s all, thank you. [He puts on the receiver—to himself, acidly.] A hundred and eighty pounds gone bang.
Look here, Dickie, now that you have a moment to spare you might give me a little professional advice. Of course, I shan’t pay you.
Good Lord! I might as well be a hospital. I’m not even supported by voluntary contributions.
The fact is, I’ve noticed lately that I’m not so thin as I was.
It can’t have required great perspicacity to notice that.
I’m not asking you for repartee, Dickie, but advice.
You don’t want to bother about a figure at your time of life.
To tell you the truth, I have an inkling that I’ve made something of an impression on a very charming lady....
[Interrupting.] Take my advice and marry her quickly before the impression wears off.
Strange as it may appear to you, she’s a married woman.

My dear Uncle Davenport, I’m young enough to be your son; philandering with a married woman is the most exaggerated form of amusement that’s ever been invented. Take care! That’s all I say. Take care!

She’ll bind you hand and foot, and put a halter round your neck and lead you about by it. She’ll ask you ten times a day if you love her, and each time you get up to go away she’ll make a scene to force you to stay longer. Each time you put on your hat she’ll pin you down to the exact hour of your next visit.
But all women do that. It only shows that they like you.

Yes, I suppose all women do that—except Pen. Pen never bothers. She never asks you if you love her. She never keeps you when you want to get away. She never insists on knowing all your movements. And when you leave her she never asks that fatal, fiendish question, at what time will you be back?
Well, my boy, if my wife were as indifferent to me as that, I should ask myself who the other feller was.
What the dickens do you mean by that?
My dear Dickie, it’s woman’s nature to be exacting. If she’s in love with you she’s always a nuisance, and a very charming nuisance too, to my mind. I like it.
You are not suggesting that Penelope....
Now, my dear boy, I didn’t come to talk to you about Penelope, but about my own health.
[Impatiently.] Oh, you’ve got chronic adiposity. That’s all that’s the matter with you.
Good gracious me, that sounds very alarming. And what shall I do for it?

[Savagely, very quickly.] Give up wines, spirits and liqueurs, bread, butter, milk, cream, sugar, potatoes, carrots, cauliflowers, peas, turnips, rice, sago, tapioca, macaroni, jam, honey, and marmalade.
But that’s not treatment, that’s homicide!
[Taking no notice.] Put on a sweater and run round the park every morning before breakfast. Let’s have a look at your liver.
Lie down on that sofa. Now don’t make a fuss about it. I’m not going to kill you. [Barlow lies down.] Put your knees up.
[As Dickie feels his liver.] She’s a fine, dashing woman. There’s no doubt about that.
Let yourself go quite loose. Who’s a fine, dashing woman?
[Dickie starts. He gives Barlow a look, and then walks away, open-mouthed.
[Much alarmed he gets off the sofa.
[Completely abstracted.] It’s in a beastly state. I thought it would be.
[In tragic tones.] Richard, tell me the worst at once.
[Impatiently.] Don’t be such an old donkey. Your liver’s as right as mine is. There’s nothing the matter with you except that you do yourself too well, and don’t take enough exercise.
[With unction.] I suppose one has to pay for being the most popular diner-out of one’s time.
[Looking at him sharply.] Is it on Mrs. Fergusson that you’ve made something of an impression?
[With great self-satisfaction.] My dear fellow, I am the last man to give a woman away.
Between ourselves, Dickie, do you think Mrs. Fergusson would find it peculiar if I asked her to lunch with me tête-à-tête at the Carlton?
Do you think her husband would mind?
Oh, her husband’s all right. He keeps on bravely serving his country in a foreign land.
It shows that she has a nice nature, or she wouldn’t have come to ask Penelope if she minded your going to Paris together.
Yes, she has a charming nature.
Lucky dog, I wish I were going to Paris with her.
Ha, ha. Well, well, I must be running away. I’m dining out as usual. These good duchesses, they will not leave me alone. Good-bye.
[He goes out. Dickie walks up and down the room thinking. In a moment Penelope puts her head in.
